# Polytec VibroFlex QTec Single-Point LDV — Characterization Protocol for Tensegrity-Inspired Energy Absorbers

## (a) Raw Observables and Derived Quantities

The fundamental raw observable of a heterodyne single-point LDV is the interferometric photocurrent produced at the detector, which carries a carrier at the Bragg cell frequency modulated in both phase and frequency by target motion. The optical phase φ(t) = (4π/λ)·s(t) encodes displacement, while the instantaneous Doppler frequency f_D(t) = (2v/λ) is directly proportional to line-of-sight velocity (chiariotti2020laserdopplervibrometry pages 11-14, chiariotti2020laserdopplervibrometry pages 4-7). Digital demodulation recovers velocity via frequency demodulation (FDM) and displacement via phase demodulation (PDM); in the QTec's 100 kHz configuration, velocity is the primary calibrated output (bauer2002highprecisionlaservibrometers pages 1-2).

From these raw observables, the following quantities are derived:

- **Velocity v(t)**: Direct FDM output; no further integration needed. Units: m/s.
- **Displacement s(t)**: Time-integration of v(t) after detrending and high-pass conditioning to suppress low-frequency drift, or direct PDM. Units: m (chiariotti2020laserdopplervibrometry pages 11-14, hansche2007widefieldlaserdoppler pages 9-13).
- **Acceleration a(t)**: Numerical differentiation of v(t) with prior low-pass smoothing to control noise amplification. Units: m/s² or g (chiariotti2020laserdopplervibrometry pages 4-7).
- **Transmitted force/pressure (gas-gun deployment)**: Back-face particle-velocity history is converted to transmitted stress σ(t) = ρ·c·v_particle(t) under 1-D wave assumptions, where ρc is the acoustic impedance of the target plate material. Force follows as F = σ·A (ramesh1990dynamicbehaviorof pages 3-4, ramesh1990dynamicbehaviorof pages 6-8, rajendran2003criticalmeasurementsfor pages 1-4).
- **Operating deflection shapes (ODS)**: By sweeping the single-point beam across a grid between nominally repeatable shots, velocity FRFs at each point are assembled to reconstruct spatial vibration patterns without mass loading (nutakor2015layeredsheetsteeldamping pages 3-4, stanbridge1999modaltestingusing pages 1-3).
- **Transmissibility T(f)**: Ratio of output-to-input velocity spectra, requiring a reference channel on the excitation side (nutakor2015layeredsheetsteeldamping pages 3-4, nutakor2015layeredsheetsteeldamping pages 2-3).
- **Damping ratio ζ and loss factor η**: Extracted from LDV-derived FRFs via the half-power bandwidth method around resonance peaks; for lightly damped modes, η ≈ 2ζ (nutakor2015layeredsheetsteeldamping pages 3-4, scalzo2023influenceofthe pages 7-10).

The following table summarizes these observables and their processing chains:

| Observable/Quantity | Description | Derivation/Processing Step | Units |
|---|---|---|---|
| Raw interferometric photocurrent / heterodyne Doppler signal | Primary LDV output: detector current / voltage containing the Bragg carrier and motion-induced phase or frequency modulation; optical phase encodes displacement and instantaneous Doppler frequency encodes line-of-sight motion (chiariotti2020laserdopplervibrometry pages 11-14, chiariotti2020laserdopplervibrometry pages 4-7, bauer2002highprecisionlaservibrometers pages 1-2) | Photodetection of interference between reference and measurement beams; down-mixing / demodulation and band-limited filtering in the vibrometer front-end before export to DAQ (chiariotti2020laserdopplervibrometry pages 11-14, bauer2002highprecisionlaservibrometers pages 1-2) | A or V |
| Velocity | Fundamental mechanical observable of a single-point LDV; line-of-sight surface velocity proportional to Doppler frequency shift (chiariotti2020laserdopplervibrometry pages 4-7, hansche2007widefieldlaserdoppler pages 15-17, nutakor2015layeredsheetsteeldamping pages 2-3) | Frequency demodulation of the heterodyne signal, with projection correction if the beam is not normal to the motion direction; use anti-aliased time history or FFT spectra as needed (chiariotti2020laserdopplervibrometry pages 11-14, lea2015twowavephotondoppler pages 2-3, nutakor2015layeredsheetsteeldamping pages 2-3) | m/s |
| Displacement | Surface displacement history at the measured point; also encoded in accumulated optical phase (chiariotti2020laserdopplervibrometry pages 11-14, hansche2007widefieldlaserdoppler pages 13-15) | Either phase demodulation directly from the interferometric signal, or numerical time-integration of velocity after detrending / high-pass conditioning to suppress drift and low-frequency bias (chiariotti2020laserdopplervibrometry pages 11-14, hansche2007widefieldlaserdoppler pages 9-13, rothberg2004laservibrometrymeets pages 11-12) | m |
| Acceleration | Point acceleration history used to compare with accelerometer data or compute transmitted g-levels (chiariotti2020laserdopplervibrometry pages 4-7) | Numerical differentiation of velocity in time, typically after low-pass filtering / smoothing to control noise amplification; equivalently second derivative of phase-derived displacement (chiariotti2020laserdopplervibrometry pages 4-7, hansche2007widefieldlaserdoppler pages 13-15) | m/s^2 or g |
| Transmitted force | For impact / gas-gun use, back-face particle-velocity history can be converted to transmitted force or stress/pressure using impedance relations under 1-D wave assumptions (ramesh1990dynamicbehaviorof pages 3-4, ramesh1990dynamicbehaviorof pages 6-8, lea2015twowavephotondoppler pages 1-2, rajendran2003criticalmeasurementsfor pages 1-4) | Measure back-face velocity history, correct for beam angle if needed, window the interferogram / spectrum, then back-compute stress or pressure via bar or plate impedance relations; multiply stress by loaded area to obtain force where appropriate (ramesh1990dynamicbehaviorof pages 6-8, lea2015twowavephotondoppler pages 2-3, rajendran2003criticalmeasurementsfor pages 1-4) | N, Pa, or MPa |
| Operating deflection shapes | Spatial vibration shape of the specimen under a chosen excitation or impact condition, assembled from many single-point measurements without mass loading (nutakor2015layeredsheetsteeldamping pages 3-4, johansmann2005anewtool pages 1-2, stanbridge1999modaltestingusing pages 1-3) | Sweep the single-point LDV across a grid between nominally repeatable shots or harmonic excitations; store velocity FRFs or spectra at each point and reconstruct ODS / mode-shape fields from amplitude and phase maps (nutakor2015layeredsheetsteeldamping pages 3-4, yuan2022inplaneoperatingdeflection pages 1-2, stanbridge1999modaltestingusing pages 1-3) | Relative amplitude/phase, or m/s or m |
| Transmissibility | Frequency-domain ratio showing how much vibration is transmitted through the absorber from input point / fixture to output point / target face (nutakor2015layeredsheetsteeldamping pages 3-4, nutakor2015layeredsheetsteeldamping pages 2-3) | Compute FRFs or velocity spectra at output and input points, then form magnitude or complex ratio T(f) = V_out(f) / V_in(f); coherence checking is recommended before interpreting peaks / valleys (nutakor2015layeredsheetsteeldamping pages 3-4, nutakor2015layeredsheetsteeldamping pages 2-3) | Dimensionless or dB |
| Damping ratio zeta | Modal damping descriptor for a resonance of the tensegrity / lattice specimen (nutakor2015layeredsheetsteeldamping pages 3-4, scalzo2023influenceofthe pages 7-10, scalzo2023influenceofthe pages 6-7) | Extract from LDV-derived FRF using half-power bandwidth around a resonance, zeta ~= (f2 - f1) / (2 fn), or by fitting a viscous single-DOF model to the resonance peak / compliance curve (nutakor2015layeredsheetsteeldamping pages 3-4, scalzo2023influenceofthe pages 7-10, scalzo2023influenceofthe pages 6-7) | Dimensionless |
| Loss factor eta | Alternative damping metric commonly reported for architected / lattice materials and modal tests (nutakor2015layeredsheetsteeldamping pages 3-4, nutakor2015layeredsheetsteeldamping pages 1-2) | Derive from the same resonance-bandwidth or curve-fit procedure used for damping; for lightly damped modes, eta ~= 2 zeta (nutakor2015layeredsheetsteeldamping pages 3-4, nutakor2015layeredsheetsteeldamping pages 1-2) | Dimensionless |


*Table: This table summarizes the direct outputs of a single-point LDV and the main derived quantities relevant to impact and vibration characterization of the tensegrity absorber. It is useful for defining BO-ready metrics and the associated processing steps.*

## (b) Derived Quantities as Bayesian-Optimization Objectives

**Peak transmitted acceleration / force (g_max / F_peak).** The LDV on the drop-tower side provides a non-contact velocity history from which acceleration is differentiated and peak g is extracted. Because the LDV imposes zero mass loading, it avoids the bias inherent in IEPE accelerometers on small or compliant specimens (scalzo2023influenceofthe pages 7-10, scalzo2023influenceofthe pages 6-7). On the gas-gun side, the back-face velocity yields peak transmitted force via impedance relations (lea2015twowavephotondoppler pages 1-2, rajendran2003criticalmeasurementsfor pages 1-4). F_peak (or g_max) is a strong minimize-objective candidate with typical noise floors set by speckle: broadband velocity noise of order 1–7 mm/s for non-ideal surfaces (rothberg2004laservibrometrymeets pages 9-11), which propagates to ~0.5–5 g noise after differentiation at 100 kHz bandwidth. Repeatability (CoV) across nominally identical shots should be assessed from ≥3 replicates; tensegrity-inspired structures show absorbed-momentum repeatability within 1% (pajunen2019designandimpact pages 7-8), suggesting that LDV-derived F_peak CoV < 5% is achievable with proper surface preparation.

**Specific energy absorption (SEA).** SEA = VEA/ρ_s where VEA = ∫₀^{ε_d} σ(ε)dε, with σ computed from LDV velocity via impedance and ε from integration or complementary displacement data (cronau2025energyabsorptionof pages 2-4). For polymer lattices at 25% relative density, SEA values are the highest among tested densities in stochastic lattice studies (cronau2025energyabsorptionof pages 1-2). Units: J/g. SEA is a strong maximize-objective; CoV is typically 5–10% in AM lattices due to print variability.

**Crush / plateau efficiency η.** Defined as η = σ_pl / σ_p (inverse of the overshoot ratio O = σ_p / σ_pl) (cronau2025energyabsorptionof pages 2-4). Ideal is η = 1.0. The LDV-derived force–time history directly provides σ_p and σ_pl. This is a maximize-objective.

**Energy-absorption efficiency W_min.** For tensegrity-inspired structures, Pajunen et al. define W_min = C_min · q_r, where C_min is the cushion factor (minimum = 1) and q_r is relative density. Target region: W_min < 0.21 at q_r < 0.1 (pajunen2019designandimpact pages 7-8, pajunen2019designandimpact pages 8-9). This compound metric can serve as a minimize-objective.

**Transmissibility / loss factor.** Measurable via LDV FRFs between shots using hammer or shaker excitation. Transmissibility at resonance and the loss factor η (from half-power bandwidth) characterize vibration isolation performance (nutakor2015layeredsheetsteeldamping pages 3-4, sharif2016ultralightmicrolatticematerials pages 53-59). These are secondary objectives or constraints rather than primary BO targets.

**Settling time / damping ratio ζ.** The LDV ring-down after impact provides settling time directly; ζ is extracted from FRF peak widths. For SLM lattices, contact-sensor damping can exceed intrinsic damping by two orders of magnitude, making non-contact LDV essential for accurate ζ estimation (scalzo2023influenceofthe pages 7-10, scalzo2023influenceofthe pages 6-7). ζ is best treated as a secondary objective or constraint.

**Cycle / reuse count N_reuse.** LDV displacement integration yields residual strain per impact; tensegrity-inspired structures show <0.2% remaining strain per impact and ~2.3% cumulative after 24 impacts (pajunen2019designandimpact pages 7-8, pajunen2019designandimpact pages 5-7). N_reuse (number of impacts before a threshold residual strain is exceeded) is a candidate maximize-objective, tracked by monitoring LDV-derived residual displacement across repeated shots.

**Densification strain ε_d.** Identified from the force–displacement curve as the strain at which the stress begins to rise steeply above the plateau. Derived from LDV velocity integration (drop-tower) or impedance-based stress–strain (gas-gun). Better cast as a constraint than an objective.

## (c) Quantities Better Cast as Constraints

Several derived quantities are more naturally expressed as hard cutoffs or chance-constraints in the qNEHVI formulation:

- **Peak acceleration g_max ≤ threshold.** For the egg-drop framing (ASTM D5276), the payload must survive; typical fragility thresholds for eggs are ~25–30 g. For the crutch-tip application, peak transmitted force should remain below injury-relevant thresholds. This is a hard constraint.
- **Densification strain ε_d ≥ minimum.** The absorber must not bottom out within the design stroke. For tensegrity-inspired structures, the buckling plateau should extend to at least 30–50% engineering strain before densification (pajunen2019designandimpact pages 7-8, zhang2021optimizationforenergy pages 7-11). Constraint: ε_d ≥ 0.3.
- **Residual strain per impact ≤ threshold.** Pajunen et al. report <0.2% per impact as achieved (pajunen2019designandimpact pages 7-8). A constraint of ε_residual ≤ 1% per impact preserves reusability.
- **Relative density q_r ≤ 0.25.** Bounding-box mass constraint from the project specification (≤500 g in a ~200 mm sphere). Cronau & Engstler found 25% density optimal for SEA in stochastic polymer lattices (cronau2025energyabsorptionof pages 1-2).
- **Force overshoot O ≤ threshold.** The ratio σ_p/σ_pl should remain below ~1.5 to avoid damaging payloads with an initial spike; ideal O = 1.0 (cronau2025energyabsorptionof pages 2-4). Graded lattices can reduce the initial force peak but may decrease overall SEA (cronau2025energyabsorptionof pages 1-2).
- **N_reuse ≥ minimum.** For the crutch-tip framing, multi-use is required. Setting N_reuse ≥ 10 as a constraint is defensible given the demonstrated 24-impact resilience of tensegrity-inspired unit cells (pajunen2019designandimpact pages 7-8, pajunen2019designandimpact pages 5-7).
- **Minimum printable feature size.** AM constraint: minimum strut diameter ≥ 0.8 mm for SLS (cronau2025energyabsorptionof pages 2-4); comparable limits apply to FFF/Bambu H2D dual extrusion with PETG/TPU.

## (d) Recommended Characterization Settings

The following table provides literature- and standards-grounded settings for both the drop-tower and gas-gun LDV deployments:

| Parameter | Recommended Value | Rationale / Source |
|---|---|---|
| Sampling rate | **≥500 kS/s** for a 100 kHz measurement bandwidth; prefer **~1 MS/s** for shock / impact transients when storage allows | ISO 16063 guidance emphasizes high sampling rate, resolution, and memory for low uncertainty, and ISO 16063-41 calibration methods extend LDV use to 50 kHz and beyond; 1 MS/s is therefore a defensible oversampled acquisition rate for a 100 kHz LDV front-end, especially for short shock events (martens2008metrologyofvibration pages 12-13, martens2008metrologyofvibration pages 17-18, martens2008metrologyofvibration pages 10-12) |
| Anti-alias filter | **Analog low-pass enabled before digitization; cutoff at or below the retained analysis band and below Nyquist**. Practical choice: for a 100 kHz analyzed band, use **~100 kHz LP with ≥500 kS/s digitization** | Camera/DAQ undersampling and aliasing are explicitly identified as LDV failure modes; standards and metrology sources stress high-rate, properly filtered acquisition. The safest recommendation is to hardware-limit bandwidth before the ADC and sample comfortably above 2× bandwidth (hansche2007widefieldlaserdoppler pages 9-13, martens2008metrologyofvibration pages 17-18, lea2015twowavephotondoppler pages 2-3) |
| Transducer range / sensitivity | Use the **full ±30 m/s LDV range** for impact work; exploit LDV displacement capability for very small motions, but compute impact metrics primarily from **velocity** | LDV fundamentally measures line-of-sight velocity from Doppler shift; velocity is the most robust impact observable, while displacement and acceleration are derived numerically. High-range velocity capability is especially appropriate for back-face particle-velocity and drop-tower shock measurements (chiariotti2020laserdopplervibrometry pages 11-14, chiariotti2020laserdopplervibrometry pages 4-7, lea2015twowavephotondoppler pages 1-2, rajendran2003criticalmeasurementsfor pages 1-4) |
| Standoff distance | **0.3–1.5 m practical**, with **~1.0 m preferred** when geometry permits | Metrology guidance for laser vibrometer calibration reports a working distance of **1 m** between reflecting surface and laser head as a standard characterization condition; modest repositioning by **5–10 cm** is also recommended to escape coherence minima / dropouts (martens2008metrologyofvibration pages 15-17, chiariotti2020laserdopplervibrometry pages 19-22) |
| Trigger / pretrigger | Use a **hardware trigger** from the force transducer, drop-tower event, or optical gate; retain **≥10% pretrigger** record | Impact and modal LDV studies use instrumented hammer/force-trigger synchronization for repeatable timing. Pretrigger is needed to establish baseline and detect onset cleanly before integration / differentiation steps (nutakor2015layeredsheetsteeldamping pages 3-4, nutakor2015layeredsheetsteeldamping pages 2-3, lea2015twowavephotondoppler pages 2-3) |
| Window length | Record at least **2× expected event duration**; practical starting values: **5–20 ms** for drop-tower events and **50–200 µs** for gas-gun / bar-type transmitted-wave events | Windowing must span the full transient plus settling tail. PDV/impact studies explicitly use short overlapping windows for microsecond events, while drop / modal decay studies require millisecond-scale records to capture ring-down and damping (lea2015twowavephotondoppler pages 2-3, pajunen2019designandimpact pages 7-8, pajunen2019designandimpact pages 5-7) |
| Number of averages / repeats | **3–5 shots per specimen configuration minimum**; increase if dropout or geometric variability is evident | Repeated impacts are needed because speckle dropout, setup variability, and specimen-to-specimen differences can corrupt single-shot inference. Architected-material damping and impact studies commonly rely on replicates / repeated impacts to assess repeatability and residual strain evolution (martin2009introducingspecklenoise pages 2-3, pajunen2019designandimpact pages 7-8, scalzo2023influenceofthe pages 6-7) |
| Target preparation | Prefer a **small optically cooperative patch** on a rigid local feature (painted diffuse white or firmly bonded retro-reflective tape); verify adhesion before shock testing | Speckle noise and dropouts are dominant LDV artifacts. Rough/diffuse treatments and retro-reflective patches can improve return, but tape does **not** guarantee dropout-free data and can itself fail under impact if poorly bonded (chiariotti2020laserdopplervibrometry pages 19-22, martin2009introducingspecklenoise pages 2-3, rothberg2004laservibrometrymeets pages 9-11, martin2009introducingspecklenoise pages 3-4) |
| Mounting / boundary condition for between-shot modal work | For damping / transmissibility characterization between impacts, use **free-free or minimally intrusive support** whenever possible | Contact sensors, clamping, and wiring can add damping and shift modal properties by large amounts; non-contact LDV with free-free support gives the most defensible estimate of intrinsic lattice damping (scalzo2023influenceofthe pages 7-10, scalzo2023influenceofthe pages 6-7, scalzo2023influenceofthe pages 1-2, scalzo2023influenceofthe pages 10-12) |
| Excitation profile for characterization | For modal / damping sweeps between impacts, use **instrumented impact hammer** or **sinusoidal chirp** at small amplitude; for impact trials, measure the true shock pulse directly | Architected-material LDV literature uses pulse testing and chirp excitation for damping/modal extraction, with force reference channels for synchronization and FRF estimation (scalzo2023influenceofthe pages 7-10, nutakor2015layeredsheetsteeldamping pages 1-2, scalzo2023influenceofthe pages 6-7) |
| Standards / protocol anchor | **ISO 16063-41** for LDV calibration, **ISO 16063-13** for primary shock calibration, **ISO 16063-11** for interferometric vibration calibration; compare against accelerometer channels only as secondary references | These are the directly relevant metrology standards identified for laser vibrometers, vibration calibration, and shock calibration. They provide the strongest standards-based anchor for the LDV protocol in this lab context (martens2008metrologyofvibration pages 12-13, martens2008metrologyofvibration pages 10-12, martens2012applicabilityofiso pages 3-6) |


*Table: This table summarizes literature- and standards-grounded settings for using a single-point LDV on architected polymer impact absorbers. It is useful as a practical protocol template for drop-tower and gas-gun deployments while preserving traceability to metrology standards and known LDV failure modes.*

Key standards anchoring the protocol are ISO 16063-41 for LDV calibration (frequency range 0.4 Hz to 50 kHz, extendable to ≥100 kHz; uncertainty 0.25–1% for primary calibration) (martens2008metrologyofvibration pages 12-13, martens2008metrologyofvibration pages 10-12), ISO 16063-13 for primary shock calibration (pulse durations 0.05–10 ms, peak ranges 10²–10⁵ m/s²; uncertainty 1–2%) (martens2008metrologyofvibration pages 12-13), and ISO 16063-11 for interferometric vibration calibration (1 Hz to 10 kHz; uncertainty 0.5–1%) (martens2008metrologyofvibration pages 12-13, martens2012applicabilityofiso pages 3-6). The metrology literature recommends a standoff of ~1.0 m, environmental conditions of 23 °C ± 3 K, and acquisition at the highest feasible sampling rate with large memory (martens2008metrologyofvibration pages 15-17, martens2008metrologyofvibration pages 17-18).

For between-shot modal characterization, free-free boundary conditions (specimen suspended on nylon threads at nodal points) with non-contact LDV and instrumented hammer excitation are essential; this configuration yields damping estimates orders of magnitude more accurate than clamped/accelerometer-based setups (scalzo2023influenceofthe pages 7-10, scalzo2023influenceofthe pages 6-7, scalzo2023influenceofthe pages 1-2).

## (e) Integration into the BO Campaign (PR #30 + PR #33)

**Ax Metric / Objective shape.** Each LDV-measured shot produces scalar metrics (F_peak, SEA, η, ζ, ε_residual, N_reuse) after signal processing. These map to Ax `Metric` objects with `lower_is_better=True` for F_peak and W_min, and `lower_is_better=False` for SEA and η. The qNEHVI acquisition function handles the multi-objective Pareto front (pires2024datadrivendesignand pages 135-139, gorguluarslan2022multiobjectivedesignoptimization pages 1-2).

**Observation noise model.** LDV-derived metrics exhibit heteroscedastic noise: speckle dropout probability, surface quality, and specimen geometry all modulate noise per-trial. A heteroscedastic Gaussian likelihood (or inferred noise via a `MultiTaskGP` with an observation-noise kernel) is recommended. Shot-to-shot CoV should be estimated from replicate groups and fed as per-observation noise to the GP. For well-prepared specimens, velocity CoV < 3% is achievable; for SEA (which compounds force and displacement uncertainties), assume CoV ~ 5–10%.

**Per-trial cost / wall-clock budget.** A single drop-tower LDV shot requires ~2–5 min including specimen placement, laser alignment, trigger setup, and data verification. The gas-gun deployment is comparable but may require more extensive target preparation. Between-shot modal sweeps (poor-man's scanning) add ~10–30 min per specimen for a 20–50 point grid. In a BO campaign budget of ~50–100 physical trials, each LDV-augmented trial costs ~15–40 min wall-clock.

**Fidelity tier.** LDV-augmented physical impact tests constitute the highest-fidelity tier (Regime A or A+) in the multifidelity ladder. **Complementarity with other data sources.** The LDV uniquely provides: (1) non-contact, zero-mass-loading validation of the IEPE accelerometer for very small or compliant specimens; (2) back-face particle-velocity for transmitted-pressure reconstruction on the gas-gun side; and (3) between-shot ODS / modal data that no other single instrument in the lab provides. # Polytec VibroFlex QTec Single-Point LDV — Characterization Protocol for Tensegrity-Inspired Energy Absorbers

## (a) Raw Observables and Derived Quantities

The fundamental raw observable of a heterodyne single-point LDV is the interferometric photocurrent produced at the detector, which carries a carrier at the Bragg cell frequency modulated in both phase and frequency by target motion. The optical phase φ(t) = (4π/λ)·s(t) encodes displacement, while the instantaneous Doppler frequency f_D(t) = (2v/λ) is directly proportional to line-of-sight velocity (chiariotti2020laserdopplervibrometry pages 11-14, chiariotti2020laserdopplervibrometry pages 4-7). Digital demodulation recovers velocity via frequency demodulation (FDM) and displacement via phase demodulation (PDM); in the QTec's 100 kHz configuration, velocity is the primary calibrated output (bauer2002highprecisionlaservibrometers pages 1-2).

From these raw observables, the following quantities are derived:

- **Velocity v(t)**: Direct FDM output; no further integration needed. Units: m/s.
- **Displacement s(t)**: Time-integration of v(t) after detrending and high-pass conditioning to suppress low-frequency drift, or direct PDM. Units: m (chiariotti2020laserdopplervibrometry pages 11-14, hansche2007widefieldlaserdoppler pages 9-13).
- **Acceleration a(t)**: Numerical differentiation of v(t) with prior low-pass smoothing to control noise amplification. Units: m/s² or g (chiariotti2020laserdopplervibrometry pages 4-7).
- **Transmitted force/pressure (gas-gun deployment)**: Back-face particle-velocity history is converted to transmitted stress σ(t) = ρ·c·v_particle(t) under 1-D wave assumptions, where ρc is the acoustic impedance of the target plate material. Force follows as F = σ·A (ramesh1990dynamicbehaviorof pages 3-4, ramesh1990dynamicbehaviorof pages 6-8, rajendran2003criticalmeasurementsfor pages 1-4).
- **Operating deflection shapes (ODS)**: By sweeping the single-point beam across a grid between nominally repeatable shots, velocity FRFs at each point are assembled to reconstruct spatial vibration patterns without mass loading (nutakor2015layeredsheetsteeldamping pages 3-4, stanbridge1999modaltestingusing pages 1-3).
- **Transmissibility T(f)**: Ratio of output-to-input velocity spectra, requiring a reference channel on the excitation side (nutakor2015layeredsheetsteeldamping pages 3-4, nutakor2015layeredsheetsteeldamping pages 2-3).
- **Damping ratio ζ and loss factor η**: Extracted from LDV-derived FRFs via the half-power bandwidth method around resonance peaks; for lightly damped modes, η ≈ 2ζ (nutakor2015layeredsheetsteeldamping pages 3-4, scalzo2023influenceofthe pages 7-10).

## (b) Derived Quantities as Bayesian-Optimization Objectives

**Peak transmitted acceleration / force (g_max / F_peak).** The LDV on the drop-tower side provides a non-contact velocity history from which acceleration is differentiated and peak g is extracted. Because the LDV imposes zero mass loading, it avoids the bias inherent in IEPE accelerometers on small or compliant specimens (scalzo2023influenceofthe pages 7-10, scalzo2023influenceofthe pages 6-7). On the gas-gun side, the back-face velocity yields peak transmitted force via impedance relations (lea2015twowavephotondoppler pages 1-2, rajendran2003criticalmeasurementsfor pages 1-4). F_peak (or g_max) is a strong minimize-objective candidate with typical noise floors set by speckle: broadband velocity noise of order 1–7 mm/s for non-ideal surfaces (rothberg2004laservibrometrymeets pages 9-11), which propagates to ~0.5–5 g noise after differentiation at 100 kHz bandwidth. Repeatability (CoV) across nominally identical shots should be assessed from ≥3 replicates; tensegrity-inspired structures show absorbed-momentum repeatability within 1% (pajunen2019designandimpact pages 7-8), suggesting that LDV-derived F_peak CoV < 5% is achievable with proper surface preparation.

**Specific energy absorption (SEA).** SEA = VEA/ρ_s where VEA = ∫₀^{ε_d} σ(ε)dε, with σ computed from LDV velocity via impedance and ε from integration or complementary displacement data (cronau2025energyabsorptionof pages 2-4). For polymer lattices at 25% relative density, SEA values are the highest among tested densities in stochastic lattice studies (cronau2025energyabsorptionof pages 1-2). Units: J/g. SEA is a strong maximize-objective; CoV is typically 5–10% in AM lattices due to print variability.

**Crush / plateau efficiency η.** Defined as η = σ_pl / σ_p (inverse of the overshoot ratio O = σ_p / σ_pl) (cronau2025energyabsorptionof pages 2-4). Ideal is η = 1.0. The LDV-derived force–time history directly provides σ_p and σ_pl. This is a maximize-objective.

**Energy-absorption efficiency W_min.** For tensegrity-inspired structures, Pajunen et al. define W_min = C_min · q_r, where C_min is the cushion factor (minimum = 1) and q_r is relative density. Target region: W_min < 0.21 at q_r < 0.1 (pajunen2019designandimpact pages 7-8, pajunen2019designandimpact pages 8-9). This compound metric can serve as a minimize-objective.

**Transmissibility / loss factor.** Measurable via LDV FRFs between shots using hammer or shaker excitation. Transmissibility at resonance and the loss factor η (from half-power bandwidth) characterize vibration isolation performance (nutakor2015layeredsheetsteeldamping pages 3-4, sharif2016ultralightmicrolatticematerials pages 53-59). These are secondary objectives or constraints rather than primary BO targets.

**Settling time / damping ratio ζ.** The LDV ring-down after impact provides settling time directly; ζ is extracted from FRF peak widths. For SLM lattices, contact-sensor damping can exceed intrinsic damping by two orders of magnitude, making non-contact LDV essential for accurate ζ estimation (scalzo2023influenceofthe pages 7-10, scalzo2023influenceofthe pages 6-7). ζ is best treated as a secondary objective or constraint.

**Cycle / reuse count N_reuse.** LDV displacement integration yields residual strain per impact; tensegrity-inspired structures show <0.2% remaining strain per impact and ~2.3% cumulative after 24 impacts (pajunen2019designandimpact pages 7-8, pajunen2019designandimpact pages 5-7). N_reuse (number of impacts before a threshold residual strain is exceeded) is a candidate maximize-objective, tracked by monitoring LDV-derived residual displacement across repeated shots.

**Densification strain ε_d.** Identified from the force–displacement curve as the strain at which the stress begins to rise steeply above the plateau. Derived from LDV velocity integration (drop-tower) or impedance-based stress–strain (gas-gun). Better cast as a constraint than an objective.

## (c) Quantities Better Cast as Constraints

Several derived quantities are more naturally expressed as hard cutoffs or chance-constraints in the qNEHVI formulation:

- **Peak acceleration g_max ≤ threshold.** For the egg-drop framing (ASTM D5276), the payload must survive; typical fragility thresholds for eggs are ~25–30 g. For the crutch-tip application, peak transmitted force should remain below injury-relevant thresholds. This is a hard constraint.
- **Densification strain ε_d ≥ minimum.** The absorber must not bottom out within the design stroke. For tensegrity-inspired structures, the buckling plateau should extend to at least 30–50% engineering strain before densification (pajunen2019designandimpact pages 7-8, zhang2021optimizationforenergy pages 7-11). Constraint: ε_d ≥ 0.3.
- **Residual strain per impact ≤ threshold.** Pajunen et al. report <0.2% per impact as achieved (pajunen2019designandimpact pages 7-8). A constraint of ε_residual ≤ 1% per impact preserves reusability.
- **Relative density q_r ≤ 0.25.** Bounding-box mass constraint from the project specification (≤500 g in a ~200 mm sphere). Cronau & Engstler found 25% density optimal for SEA in stochastic polymer lattices (cronau2025energyabsorptionof pages 1-2).
- **Force overshoot O ≤ threshold.** The ratio σ_p/σ_pl should remain below ~1.5 to avoid damaging payloads with an initial spike; ideal O = 1.0 (cronau2025energyabsorptionof pages 2-4). Graded lattices can reduce the initial force peak but may decrease overall SEA (cronau2025energyabsorptionof pages 1-2).
- **N_reuse ≥ minimum.** For the crutch-tip framing, multi-use is required. Setting N_reuse ≥ 10 as a constraint is defensible given the demonstrated 24-impact resilience of tensegrity-inspired unit cells (pajunen2019designandimpact pages 7-8, pajunen2019designandimpact pages 5-7).
- **Minimum printable feature size.** AM constraint: minimum strut diameter ≥ 0.8 mm for SLS (cronau2025energyabsorptionof pages 2-4); comparable limits apply to FFF/Bambu H2D dual extrusion with PETG/TPU.

## (e) Integration into the BO Campaign (PR #30 + PR #33)

**Ax Metric / Objective shape.** Each LDV-measured shot produces scalar metrics (F_peak, SEA, η, ζ, ε_residual, N_reuse) after signal processing. These map to Ax `Metric` objects with `lower_is_better=True` for F_peak and W_min, and `lower_is_better=False` for SEA and η. The qNEHVI acquisition function handles the multi-objective Pareto front (pires2024datadrivendesignand pages 135-139, gorguluarslan2022multiobjectivedesignoptimization pages 1-2).

**Observation noise model.** LDV-derived metrics exhibit heteroscedastic noise: speckle dropout probability, surface quality, and specimen geometry all modulate noise per-trial. A heteroscedastic Gaussian likelihood (or inferred noise via a `MultiTaskGP` with an observation-noise kernel) is recommended. Shot-to-shot CoV should be estimated from replicate groups and fed as per-observation noise to the GP. For well-prepared specimens, velocity CoV < 3% is achievable; for SEA (which compounds force and displacement uncertainties), assume CoV ~ 5–10%.

**Per-trial cost / wall-clock budget.** A single drop-tower LDV shot requires ~2–5 min including specimen placement, laser alignment, trigger setup, and data verification. The gas-gun deployment is comparable but may require more extensive target preparation. Between-shot modal sweeps (poor-man's scanning) add ~10–30 min per specimen for a 20–50 point grid. In a BO campaign budget of ~50–100 physical trials, each LDV-augmented trial costs ~15–40 min wall-clock.

**Fidelity tier.** LDV-augmented physical impact tests constitute the highest-fidelity tier (Regime A or A+) in the multifidelity ladder. They complement and cross-validate: (i) the drop-tower accelerometer (data source 1, which the LDV doubly checks without mass loading), (ii) the high-speed camera (data source 3, providing full-field but lower-bandwidth displacement), (iii) the gas-gun setup (data source 4, where LDV provides the back-face velocity channel), and (iv) simulation tiers (MuJoCo → Newton/Warp → PolyFEM). In a MultiTaskGP / multifidelity BO loop, LDV experimental data anchor the high-fidelity kernel while simulation predictions populate the low-fidelity task, with inter-task correlations learned automatically.

**Complementarity with other data sources.** The LDV uniquely provides: (1) non-contact, zero-mass-loading validation of the IEPE accelerometer for very small or compliant specimens; (2) back-face particle-velocity for transmitted-pressure reconstruction on the gas-gun side; and (3) between-shot ODS / modal data that no other single instrument in the lab provides. It does not replace the force transducer (direct force measurement), high-speed camera (full-field strain), or simulation (parametric sweeps), but cross-validates all of them.

## (f) Top Gotchas, Failure Modes, and Cross-Talk Artifacts

The following table ranks the 10 most critical failure modes that would silently corrupt BO objectives if ignored:

| Rank | Failure Mode / Artifact | Root Cause | Severity (High/Medium/Low) | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Speckle dropout during large specimen motion | Time-varying speckle population and low returned Doppler amplitude during rapid target rotation/translation or changing surface angle cause intermittent signal collapse and false spikes (chiariotti2020laserdopplervibrometry pages 19-22, martin2009introducingspecklenoise pages 2-3, rothberg2004laservibrometrymeets pages 11-12) | High | Use optically cooperative target patches; slightly reposition beam to a better speckle field; maximize return light; keep incidence near normal where possible; inspect time trace for dropouts and reject corrupted shots (chiariotti2020laserdopplervibrometry pages 19-22, martin2009introducingspecklenoise pages 3-4) |
| 2 | Speckle noise broadband floor | Coherent backscatter from rough surfaces produces amplitude and phase modulation; periodic motion can create pseudo-random broadband noise and harmonic contamination that masks true vibration content (martin2009introducingspecklenoise pages 2-3, rothberg2004laservibrometrymeets pages 9-11, martin2009introducingspecklenoise pages 1-2) | High | Increase optical return; use favorable surface treatment; low-pass filter to the needed bandwidth; average repeated linear tests where possible; verify coherence against an input reference (rothberg2004laservibrometrymeets pages 9-11, rothberg2004laservibrometrymeets pages 11-12, nutakor2015layeredsheetsteeldamping pages 3-4) |
| 3 | Retro-reflective tape detachment under impact | Adhesive-backed tape can debond or wrinkle under shock, creating a moving target independent of the specimen surface; retro-reflective tape also does not eliminate speckle dropouts (martin2009introducingspecklenoise pages 2-3, martin2009introducingspecklenoise pages 3-4, rothberg2004laservibrometrymeets pages 1-3) | High | Use the smallest practical, firmly bonded patch on a rigid local region; validate adhesion with sacrificial shots; prefer paint/sanded diffuse finish if tape survival is poor; never assume tape guarantees clean signal (chiariotti2020laserdopplervibrometry pages 19-22, martin2009introducingspecklenoise pages 2-3) |
| 4 | Out-of-plane motion coupling / cosine error | Single-point LDV measures only the line-of-sight velocity component; beam-target angle changes during deformation project multi-axis motion into the measured channel and bias inferred axial velocity (chiariotti2020laserdopplervibrometry pages 4-7, johansmann2005anewtool pages 1-2) | High | Align beam with the dominant motion axis; keep target plate locally normal to the beam; document incidence angle and apply projection correction if geometry is known; use multiple views or complementary sensors if large rotations occur (chiariotti2020laserdopplervibrometry pages 4-7, schell2006threedimensionalvibration pages 5-7, johansmann2005anewtool pages 1-2) |
| 5 | Window reflection parasitic signal | Measuring through a protective window introduces parasitic reflections and wavefront distortion; the vibrometer may read window vibration rather than specimen motion if reflections dominate (chiariotti2020laserdopplervibrometry pages 19-22) | High | Avoid windows if possible; otherwise use optically flat windows, tilt them to dump reflections, and verify the beam is focused on the specimen not the window; confirm with a no-impact background run (chiariotti2020laserdopplervibrometry pages 19-22) |
| 6 | TPU surface compliance / poor optical cooperativity | Soft, dark, compliant TPU surfaces can scatter weakly, deform locally, or change local surface normal, reducing return signal and worsening speckle instability on the true structural point of interest (chiariotti2020laserdopplervibrometry pages 19-22, martin2009introducingspecklenoise pages 1-2) | Medium | Measure on a rigid PETG top plate or a bonded optical target patch rather than bare TPU whenever possible; use diffuse white coating or a stable reflective spot that adds negligible mass relative to the structure (chiariotti2020laserdopplervibrometry pages 19-22, nutakor2015layeredsheetsteeldamping pages 2-3) |
| 7 | Laser beam walk-off during large displacements | Large transient motions or rotations move the illuminated spot off the intended point/plate, changing the measured location mid-shot and possibly losing the target entirely (chiariotti2020laserdopplervibrometry pages 19-22, stanbridge1999modaltestingusing pages 1-3) | High | Use a larger rigid target plate than the laser spot wander envelope; pre-align for maximum expected excursion; validate with video; limit tests to displacements that stay within the target patch for trustworthy single-point histories (chiariotti2020laserdopplervibrometry pages 19-22) |
| 8 | DAQ aliasing from inadequate anti-alias filtering | Under-sampled LDV outputs or insufficient analog filtering fold high-frequency shock content into the recorded band, corrupting velocity peaks and derived displacement/acceleration (hansche2007widefieldlaserdoppler pages 9-13, martens2008metrologyofvibration pages 17-18, lea2015twowavephotondoppler pages 2-3) | High | Sample comfortably above the highest retained frequency content and enforce analog anti-alias filtering before digitization; for windowed spectral velocimetry, choose FFT window/overlap consistent with event duration and bandwidth (hansche2007widefieldlaserdoppler pages 9-13, martens2008metrologyofvibration pages 17-18, lea2015twowavephotondoppler pages 2-3) |
| 9 | Integration drift when computing displacement from velocity | Displacement from velocity integration accumulates DC bias, low-frequency noise, and baseline errors; shock records with offsets can produce nonphysical residual displacements (chiariotti2020laserdopplervibrometry pages 11-14, rothberg2004laservibrometrymeets pages 11-12) | Medium | Prefer phase-demodulated displacement when available; otherwise detrend, baseline-correct, high-pass or band-limit before integration, and enforce physically justified start/end conditions over a bounded time window (chiariotti2020laserdopplervibrometry pages 11-14, chiariotti2020laserdopplervibrometry pages 4-7, bauer2002highprecisionlaservibrometers pages 1-2) |
| 10 | Cross-talk between drop-tower / fixture vibration and specimen signal | The LDV can capture rigid-body motion of the platen, fixture, or surrounding structure superposed on specimen deformation; contact fixtures and external damping sources can also bias dynamic metrics (scalzo2023influenceofthe pages 7-10, scalzo2023influenceofthe pages 1-2, scalzo2023influenceofthe pages 10-12) | Medium | Aim at a specimen-specific target point and use a reference channel on the drive/fixture to compute transmissibility or subtract common motion; use free-free or minimally intrusive support for modal work between shots; inspect coherence and compare against accelerometer/platen channels (nutakor2015layeredsheetsteeldamping pages 3-4, scalzo2023influenceofthe pages 7-10, scalzo2023influenceofthe pages 1-2) |
